To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

zinc mesoporphynin and heme (iron‐protoporphyrin), in nanomolar concentrations, can repress δ‐aminolevlinate synthase in cultured liver cells, that this repression occurs after induction of δaminolevulniate synthase by a variety of agents, that the effect of heme on δ‐aminolvelinate synthase is closely related to the ability of heme and metaloporphyrins to inhibit heme oxidase, that
zinc‐, tin‐ and copper‐chelated porphyins inhibit the rate‐controllling enzyme of heme biosynthesis, δ‐aminobenzulinate synthase in chick embryo liver cells.

zinc mesoporphynin and heme decrease the activity of δ‐Aminolevulinate Synthase (δ‐ALAS) in chick embryo liver cells, and the decrease is closely correlated with their ability to inhibit heme Oxygenase (HO).
In summary, our research is concerned with
the regulation of hepatic δ-aminolevulina te synthase, the first enzyme of heme biosynthesis.
the role of δ‐aminobenzic acid synthase in the regulation of heme synthesis and with the use of heme and metal‐chelated porphyins in the treatment of patients with porphyria.
understanding the molecular and cellular basis of the regulation of hepatic δ-aminolevuline synthase, the key enzyme of heme biosynthesis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
zinc and tin chelated metalloprophyrins, in combination with heme, decrease δ‐aminolevinic acid synthase activity.
heme and zinc‐mesoporphyrin in combination, at nanomolar concentrations, decrease the activity of δ‐amino-levulinic acid synthetase in chick liver cells.
heme and zinc‐chelated porphyin inhibit δ‐aminoleulinate synthase and this inhibition is related to the inhibition of heme oxygenease.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

heme is a negative feedback regulator of δ‐aminobenzulinate synthase and that the metalloporphryins are inhibitors of heme oxygenas and that the two effects are additive in reducing the activity of δ‐aminolevulinate synthase.
the repressive effects of heme and metal chelated porphryins on hepatic δ‐ALA synthase are closely related to their abilities to inhibit HO.
the effects of metalloporphryns on hepatic δ‐ALAS activity are closely related to their ability to inhibit hemeoxygenase.
The main takeaway from our work is that
zinc‐mesoporphyrin is the most effective inhibitor of heme oxygenases and the most effective inhibitor in reducing the synthesis of delta aminolevulinic acid synthase.
the porphyrias, which have been considered rare disorders for many decades, are actually much more common than previously thought, with an incidence of 1 in 10,000.
heme‐and metalloporphinyrins are known to reduce activity of δ‐amino‐levulinate synthase in liver.
